content.text: Clean Architecture, as Robert C. Martin describes it, is one rule: source code dependencies point inward, toward business policy, and never out toward the web, the database or a framework. Domain, Application, Infrastructure and Api projects are one way to enforce that rule, but they don't guarantee it. A solution can have all four and still break it, and a single project can follow it.

A team adds a message consumer that has to place orders too: the same use case, triggered by a queue instead of a POST. The solution looks like the textbook, with Domain, Application, Infrastructure and Api projects and references pointing the right way. Yet
can't be called from the worker. It reads the user from
, and the Application project compiles only because someone added a framework reference to ASP.NET Core months ago. Four projects, and the business logic still depends on the web.
The belief: Clean Architecture is a solution layout. Create Domain, Application, Infrastructure and Api projects, point the project references inward, and the architecture is clean.

It's easy to see where this comes from. Popular templates ship exactly that shape, and Microsoft's architecture guide shows its Application Core, Infrastructure and UI layers as projects. The famous diagram has four circles, so four projects is a natural mapping. Projects are visible in the solution explorer, easy to review, and the compiler enforces their references, which feels like a guarantee.
The half-truth: projects are a good way to enforce the rule. They aren't the rule.
One rule: dependencies point toward policy

Martin's 2012 post draws concentric circles: entities with enterprise-wide business rules at the center, use cases around them, interface adapters next, and frameworks and drivers outside, where the web and the database live as details. The

holds it together: source code dependencies point only inward. Inner code doesn't mention anything declared in an outer circle, whether that's a class, a function, a variable or a data format a framework defines.
Calls go out, dependencies still point in
A use case still needs the current user, the database and the email server. It gets them through

: the inner layer declares an interface for what it needs, and an outer layer implements it. At run time the call flows outward; at compile time the outer code depends on the inner interface. Microsoft's guide describes the same arrangement: abstractions defined in the Application Core, implemented by types in Infrastructure, and connected with
. That's why the guide lets the web project reference Infrastructure, but only for that wiring.

Martin says so directly: the circles are schematic, you may need more than four, and the one constant is that the Dependency Rule always applies. Microsoft's guide adds that layers are a logical separation. A single-project app can separate concerns with folders. Splitting into projects adds something specific: the compiler checks that each project uses only the projects it references.
Projects check references, not the rule

That check is narrower than it looks. Nothing stops someone adding a framework reference to ASP.NET Core or a package reference to EF Core in the Application project, and from then on the compiler lets inner code name
without complaint. Martin's advice to pass simple data structures across boundaries, rather than entities or database rows, is also beyond what a project reference can check.
The fix: let the inner circle own what it needs

content.text: This is our view, not a rule from the sources: for a small service, one project with clear folders and an architecture test in CI is often enough. Separate projects pay off when you want the compiler to guard the direction, or when several teams or modules share the core. Either way, choose on purpose.

content.text: Current user, clock, email, payments, file storage: declare an interface in the inner layer, implement it in the outer layer, and register it in
Endpoints map requests to commands and results to status codes. Use cases take plain input and return plain results.
Use separate projects for a compile-time check, or an architecture test in CI for a single project, and review every new reference added to inner code.

items.text: Clean Architecture is one rule: source code dependencies point inward, toward business policy.
The circles, and the four projects, are schematic; the Dependency Rule is what always applies.
Projects make the compiler check project references, nothing more; a package or framework reference can still break the rule.
Calls flow outward at run time through interfaces the inner layer owns, wired up in the composition root.
If a use case can't run without the web or the database, the arrows point the wrong way.
